summary.text: A recurrence invariant gives \(a(n)=(5n-4)/\gcd(5n-4,B_n(3))\); choosing \(n_0<p\) with \(5n_0\equiv4\pmod p\), factorial identities show that this gcd is exactly \((5n_0-4)/p\) (with the \(p=11,n_0=3\) case handled directly). Conversely, a factorial divisibility and \(p\)-adic valuation argument rules out any occurrence at \(n\ge p\), after which cancellation in \(5n\equiv4\pmod p\) makes the index unique.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac1{\displaystyle 2-\frac3{\displaystyle 3-\frac4{\displaystyle 4-\frac5{\ddots-\frac n{n+4}}}}}}
\qquad(n\ge 3),
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the denominator of \(C_n\) in lowest terms. We prove that every odd prime \(p\ne3,5\) is equal to \(a(n)\) for exactly one \(n\ge3\).

Throughout the proof, factorials are factorials of nonnegative integers, and divisibility statements involving the auxiliary quantities below may be read in \(\mathbb Z\).

## 1. A continuant for the continued fraction

Fix \(n\ge4\). Define integers \(B_{n,k}\) downward from the top of the continued fraction by
\[
B_{n,n}=n+4,
\qquad
B_{n,n-1}=n^2+2n-4,
\]
and, for \(k+1<n\),
\[
B_{n,k}=kB_{n,k+1}-(k+1)B_{n,k+2}.                 \tag{1}
\]
The first two values are chosen because
\[
(n-1)-\frac n{n+4}
 =\frac{(n-1)(n+4)-n}{n+4}
 =\frac{n^2+2n-4}{n+4}.
\]
Thus, if \(T_{n,k}\) denotes the tail beginning at \(k\), then induction downward using (1) gives
\[
T_{n,k}=k-\frac{k+1}{T_{n,k+1}}
       =\frac{B_{n,k}}{B_{n,k+1}}.                 \tag{2}
\]
We will justify that none of the denominators in this calculation vanish by proving positivity below.

The key invariant is
\[
(k-1)B_{n,k}-k(k-2)B_{n,k+1}=5n-4                 \tag{3}
\]
for \(2\le k\le n-1\). At \(k=n-1\), substituting the two top values gives
\[
(n-2)(n^2+2n-4)-(n-1)(n-3)(n+4)=5n-4.
\]
If (3) is known at \(k+1\), then substitution of (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(k-1)B_{n,k}-k(k-2)B_{n,k+1}\\
&=(k-1)\bigl(kB_{n,k+1}-(k+1)B_{n,k+2}\bigr)
       -k(k-2)B_{n,k+1}\\
&=kB_{n,k+1}-(k^2-1)B_{n,k+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is precisely the left side of (3) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\). Hence (3) follows by downward induction.

This invariant also proves positivity. The top value \(B_{n,n-1}=n^2+2n-4\) is positive. If \(B_{n,k+1}>0\) and \(k\ge2\), then (3) can be rearranged as
\[
(k-1)B_{n,k}=5n-4+k(k-2)B_{n,k+1}>0.
\]
Since \(k-1>0\), it follows that \(B_{n,k}>0\). Thus all the quantities used in (2) are nonzero.

At \(k=3\), (3) reads
\[
2B_{n,3}-3B_{n,4}=5n-4.                            \tag{4}
\]
Using (2) and then (4), the entire continued fraction is
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_n
 &=\frac1{2-3/T_{n,3}}
  =\frac1{2-3B_{n,4}/B_{n,3}}\\
 &=\frac{B_{n,3}}{2B_{n,3}-3B_{n,4}}
  =\frac{B_{n,3}}{5n-4}.                           \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently its reduced denominator is
\[
a(n)=\frac{5n-4}{\gcd(B_{n,3},5n-4)}
\qquad(n\ge4).                                    \tag{6}
\]
In particular,
\[
a(n)\mid 5n-4.                                    \tag{7}
\]
Directly from the original fraction at the first index,
\[
C_3=\frac1{2-3/7}=\frac7{11},
\qquad a(3)=11.                                   \tag{8}
\]
Also, (6) at \(n=4\) gives \(B_{4,3}=20\), hence
\[
a(4)=\frac{16}{\gcd(20,16)}=4.                   \tag{9}
\]

## 2. Two factorial identities

We need congruence information about \(B_{n,3}\). Multiply (3) by \((k-3)!\). Since
\((k-2)!=(k-2)(k-3)!\), for \(3\le k\le n-2\) this gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(k-3)!(k-1)B_{n,k}-(k-2)!kB_{n,k+1}\\
 &\hspace{35mm}=(k-3)!(5n-4).                     \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing (10) from \(k=3\) through \(n-2\) telescopes. The initial term is \(2B_{n,3}\), while the terminal term is
\[
(n-4)!(n-2)B_{n,n-1}
=(n-4)!(n-2)(n^2+2n-4).
\]
Therefore, for \(n\ge5\),
\[
\boxed{
2B_{n,3}
=(n-4)!(n-2)(n^2+2n-4)
 +(5n-4)\sum_{j=0}^{n-5}j! .}                     \tag{11}
\]
In particular,
\[
5n-4\mid
2B_{n,3}-(n-4)!(n-2)(n^2+2n-4).                  \tag{12}
\]

Multiplying (12) by \(n-2\) and using
\[
(n-1)!=(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)(n-4)!,
\]
one obtains a second useful congruence:
\[
\boxed{
5n-4\mid 2(n-2)B_{n,3}-(n+4)(n-1)! .}             \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, after the multiplication, the difference between the factorial term in (12) and \((n+4)(n-1)!\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(n-2)^2(n-4)!(n^2+2n-4)
 -(n+4)(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)(n-4)!\\
 &=(5n-4)(n-2)(n-4)!,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is itself divisible by \(5n-4\).

We will also use the elementary parity fact
\[
2\mid\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}j!\qquad(m\ge2).             \tag{14}
\]
This holds because \(0!+1!=2\), and every later factorial is even.

## 3. A prime-power factorial estimate

We next establish the estimate needed when an index is large.

**Lemma.** Let \(p\ge7\) be prime, let \(n\ge5\), and suppose \(p\le n-1\). If
\[
p^e\mid 5n-4,
\]
then
\[
p^e\mid(n-1)!.
\]

It is enough to prove
\[
e\le \left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{p}\right\rfloor,     \tag{15}
\]
because the exponent of \(p\) in \((n-1)!\) is
\[
\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
which is at least its first term.

Suppose, to the contrary, that (15) fails. Then
\(n-1<ep\), so \(n\le ep\). Since \(p^e\) is a positive divisor of \(5n-4\),
\[
p^e\le5n-4<5ep,
\]
and division by \(p\) yields
\[
p^{e-1}<5e.                                      \tag{16}
\]
For every \(e\ge3\), one has
\[
5e\le7^{e-1};                                     \tag{17}
\]
this begins with \(15\le49\) at \(e=3\), and induction follows because multiplication of the right side by \(7\) more than accommodates the increase of the left side from \(5e\) to \(5(e+1)\). Since \(p\ge7\), (17) contradicts (16). Thus \(e\le2\).

If \(e=1\), failure of (15) says \(n-1<p\), contradicting the assumption \(p\le n-1\). If \(e=2\), (16) says \(p<10\); the only prime \(p\ge7\) with this property is \(p=7\). We then have \(8\le n\le14\), while \(49\mid5n-4\). But for \(n=8,9,\ldots,14\), the numbers \(5n-4\) are
\[
36,41,46,51,56,61,66,
\]
none divisible by \(49\). This final contradiction proves (15) and the lemma.

Two simple coprimality observations will repeatedly be used. If \(p\ge7\) is prime and \(p\mid5n-4\), then
\[
p\nmid n-2,\qquad p\nmid n+4.                    \tag{18}
\]
For the first assertion, if \(p\mid n-2\), then \(p\) divides both \(5n-4\) and \(5(n-2)\), hence divides their difference \(6\), impossible for \(p\ge7\). For the second, if \(p\mid n+4\), then \(p\mid5(n+4)\), and comparison with \(5n-4\) shows that \(p\mid24\). No prime at least \(7\) divides \(24\).

## 4. What happens at a large index

Let \(p\ge7\) be prime, \(n\ge5\), and suppose
\[
p\le n-1,
\qquad p\mid5n-4.                                 \tag{19}
\]
We claim that
\[
p\nmid a(n).                                     \tag{20}
\]

Put \(m=5n-4\) and let \(e=v_p(m)\), so
\[
p^e\mid m,
\qquad p^{e+1}\nmid m.                            \tag{21}
\]
By the lemma, \(p^e\mid(n-1)!\). Congruence (13), together with \(p^e\mid m\), therefore implies
\[
p^e\mid2(n-2)B_{n,3}.
\]
By (18), \(p\nmid n-2\), and of course the odd prime \(p\) does not divide \(2\). Hence \(p^e\) is coprime to \(2(n-2)\), so
\[
p^e\mid B_{n,3}.                                 \tag{22}
\]
Thus \(p^e\) divides \(g=\gcd(B_{n,3},m)\). If \(p\) divided \(a(n)=m/g\), then multiplying \(p^e\mid g\) by \(p\mid m/g\) would give
\[
p^{e+1}\mid g\frac mg=m,
\]
contrary to (21). This proves (20).

## 5. Constructing an occurrence of a given prime

Let \(p\ge7\) be prime. Because \(5\) is invertible modulo \(p\), there is a unique residue \(n_0\), \(0\le n_0<p\), such that
\[
5n_0\equiv4\pmod p.                               \tag{23}
\]
This residue is nonzero. It is also not \(1\) or \(2\): more directly, if \(n_0\le2\), then \(5n_0-4\) is positive and smaller than \(p\) whenever it could be divisible by \(p\), which is impossible (the possibilities are \(1\) and \(6\); neither is divisible by a prime at least \(7\)). Therefore
\[
3\le n_0<p,
\qquad p\mid5n_0-4.                               \tag{24}
\]
We prove \(a(n_0)=p\).

If \(n_0=3\), then \(p\mid11\), so primality forces \(p=11\), and (8) gives \(a(3)=11=p\). The case \(n_0=4\) cannot occur: it would imply \(p\mid16\), impossible for a prime \(p\ge7\). It remains to handle
\[
5\le n_0\le p-1.                                  \tag{25}
\]
For readability, write \(n=n_0\), \(B=B_{n,3}\), and
\[
5n-4=pc.                                          \tag{26}
\]
Since \(n<p\), we have \(5n-4<5p\), and hence
\[
1\le c\le4.                                      \tag{27}
\]

First, \(p\nmid B\). For if \(p\mid B\), congruence (13) would imply
\[
p\mid(n+4)(n-1)!.
\]
The first factor is not divisible by \(p\), by (18). The second is not divisible by \(p\), since every factor in \((n-1)!\) is less than \(p\) by (25). This is a contradiction.

We next prove
\[
c\mid B                                             \tag{28}
\]
by considering the four possibilities in (27). Let
\[
S=\sum_{j=0}^{n-5}j!,
\qquad
T=(n-4)!(n-2)(n^2+2n-4).
\]
Identity (11) becomes
\[
2B=T+pcS.                                         \tag{29}
\]

* If \(c=1\), (28) is immediate.

* If \(c=2\), equation \(5n-4=2p\), with \(p\) odd, gives \(n\equiv2\pmod4\); hence \(4\mid n-2\), so \(4\mid T\). Also \(n\ge6\), and (14) gives \(2\mid S\). Therefore \(4\mid pcS\), and (29) gives \(4\mid2B\), whence \(2\mid B\).

* If \(c=3\), reducing \(5n-4=3p\) modulo \(3\) gives \(n\equiv2\pmod3\). Thus \(3\mid n-2\), so \(3\mid T\); clearly \(3\mid pcS\). Hence \(3\mid2B\). Since \(3\nmid2\), it follows that \(3\mid B\).

* If \(c=4\), reducing \(5n-4=4p\) modulo \(4\) gives \(4\mid n\). Write \(n=4r\). A direct factorization gives
\[
(n-2)(n^2+2n-4)
=8(2r-1)(4r^2+2r-1),
\]
so \(8\mid T\). Here \(n\ge8\), and (14) again gives \(2\mid S\); therefore \(8\mid4pS=pcS\). Equation (29) gives \(8\mid2B\), and hence \(4\mid B\).

This proves (28) in every case. Since \(p\nmid B\), we have \(\gcd(B,p)=1\). Combining this with \(c\mid B\) and \(5n-4=pc\),
\[
\gcd(B,5n-4)=\gcd(B,pc)=c.
\]
Formula (6) now gives
\[
a(n)=\frac{pc}{c}=p.                              \tag{30}
\]
Thus every prime \(p\ge7\) occurs at the index \(n_0\) specified by (23).

## 6. Any occurrence must be that one

Suppose \(p\ge7\) is prime, \(n\ge3\), and
\[
a(n)=p.                                          \tag{31}
\]
We show
\[
n<p,
\qquad p\mid5n-4.                                \tag{32}
\]
If \(n=3\), then (8) and (31) give \(p=11\), and (32) is immediate. If \(n=4\), (9) contradicts the primality and size of \(p\). Thus we may assume \(n\ge5\).

By (7) and (31), \(p\mid5n-4\). If \(n=p\), comparison of \(p\mid5p\) and \(p\mid5p-4\) would give \(p\mid4\), impossible. If \(n>p\), then \(p\le n-1\), and the result of Section 4 says \(p\nmid a(n)\), contradicting \(a(n)=p\). Therefore \(n<p\), proving (32).

Finally, there is at most one positive integer less than \(p\) satisfying the divisibility in (32). Indeed, if \(r,s<p\) and
\[
p\mid5r-4,
\qquad p\mid5s-4,
\]
then
\[
5r\equiv4\equiv5s\pmod p.
\]
As \(p\ne5\), multiplication by \(5\) is cancellable modulo \(p\), so \(r\equiv s\pmod p\). Since both lie between \(0\) and \(p-1\), this implies \(r=s\).

Now let \(p\) be any odd prime other than \(3\) and \(5\). Necessarily \(p\ge7\). Section 5 constructs an index \(n_0\ge3\) with \(a(n_0)=p\). If another \(n\ge3\) had \(a(n)=p\), Section 6 would show that both \(n\) and \(n_0\) are less than \(p\) and both satisfy \(5n\equiv4\pmod p\); the residue uniqueness just proved gives \(n=n_0\). Hence every odd prime other than \(3\) and \(5\) occurs exactly once among the values \(a(n)\), as claimed.
